"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 3712: an almost inert, unexplained direction.

What it is: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP output, read from hidden unit 3712 of the
MLP (its activation is about 0.24 times that unit's value, plus small terms). It is almost
never important to the model: its causal importance is near zero on every token.

What was tried (on training rows, 12k rows of 512 tokens):
- Its value is not set by the current token: a per-token lookup explains about 0 percent of
  the variance out of sample, and a token-category rule (digit, punctuation, CJK, word
  start, word continuation, byte fragment, special token) explains about 0.2 percent.
- The preceding token adds little, and a token pair table explains about 4 percent, but
  that needs a table of over a million entries, so it is not used here.
- Its position in the document, repeated tokens and counts of digits or punctuation in the
  recent window explain under 0.1 percent.

What the program does: the first token of each document gives 0 (the activation is
essentially zero there); every other position gets the component's mean, about -0.0125.
It is a baseline, not an explanation of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN = -0.0125


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, (0.0 if first else MEAN)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 3713: a diffuse, unpredictable signal.

What it does: predicts the component's typical activation everywhere, and 0 at the
first token of each document (the component is always ~0 there).

Why this simple: the component's activation (mean 0.047, std 0.28) is a sum over
thousands of MLP hidden units, with no clear trigger. Its causal importance is
essentially zero everywhere, and switching it off barely changes the output.
Token identity, token class, position, repeated-text context and bracket depth
together explain only about 1-2% of its variance out of sample, so a constant
at the mean is as good as any simple rule.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.045  # the component's average activation over ordinary tokens
FIRST_TOKEN_ACTIVATION = 0.0  # at each document's first token it is ~0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    starts_document = prefix.position == 0 or (
        prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    if starts_document:
        return carry, FIRST_TOKEN_ACTIVATION
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Negative while the text is stating or asking how one quantity affects, depends on or
changes with another.

Layer 15's MLP writes this component's output into the residual stream. Its activation is
mostly small noise, but it dips strongly negative (-2 to -15) on words that state a
cause-and-effect or dependence relation ("effect", "affects", "depends", "varies"), and
more weakly on change words ("increase", "decrease", "rate", "significantly") and on the
question and result words around them ("how", "expected", "results"). The dip fades over
roughly the next ten tokens, so the program keeps a decaying memory of those words within
a document. It predicts only that pattern; the rest of the activation is not modelled.
"""

import re

READS = ()

CAUSE = re.compile(r"(effects?|affects?|affected|depends?|dependent|dependence|influences?|influenced|impacts?|vary|varies|varied|variation)")
CHANGE = re.compile(r"(increases?|increased|decreases?|decreased|changes?|rates?|differences?|proportional|significantly)")
ASK = re.compile(r"(how|expected|results?|same|observed)")
DECAY = 0.8


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (decaying memory of relation words so far in this document, document label)
    memory, document = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != document:
        memory = 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    value = -0.2 * memory
    if CAUSE.fullmatch(word):
        value += -0.8
        memory = DECAY * memory + 1.0
    elif CHANGE.fullmatch(word):
        value += -0.2
        memory = DECAY * memory + 1.0
    elif ASK.fullmatch(word):
        value += -0.15
        memory = DECAY * memory + 1.0
    else:
        memory = DECAY * memory
    return (memory, prefix.document_ids[-1]), value

"""Predicts 0 everywhere: the component is treated as switched off.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3715 is one rank-one piece of layer 15's
MLP down projection. Its activation is the projection of the MLP's hidden units onto its
read direction: about 45% of that direction's weight sits on hidden unit 3715 and the rest is
spread over thousands of other units. It has no readable trigger. Its activation is roughly
zero-mean noise (std 0.29, rare values beyond |2|), and its causal importance never passes 0.1.
Token identity, token class, previous token and position explain almost none of it (under 2%
even with a full per-token table; a linear fit on the normalised residual reaches about 20%, but
that is the model's own computation, not a readable rule).

So this program does not describe the activation. It predicts 0 at every position, which is
what switching the component off does, and it moves the model's predictions as much as
switching it off does.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The component's activation at this position: 0, as if it were switched off."""
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3716: a diffuse readout with no readable trigger.

What it is: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its activation is a fixed
linear readout of the layer's 6144 MLP hidden units (almost all of its weight sits on many
small units; unit 3716 alone carries about 16% of its variance). Its activation is
roughly symmetric around 0 (std about 0.29), and its causal importance essentially never
passes 0.1, so the model barely uses it.

What was tried, on about 2M training tokens: the activation depends on the token only
weakly (token identity explains about 0.5% of its variance, bigrams about 1%, a
word/punctuation/digit/CJK/Cyrillic class about 0.1%), on position in the row only at the
start (position 0 is exactly 0), and on text type only a little (row averages track
digits, punctuation and whitespace, about 6% of the variance of row means). None of these
is a trigger, so the program predicts the component's mean value everywhere.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.02  # the component's mean over training text; its spread is about 0.29


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # A constant: the best a readable rule gets here, since no token or context feature
    # explains more than about 1% of the activation's variance.
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 3717: a near-silent, context-noisy component.

What it does. Its activation is a small, noisy number: mean about 0.04, spread about 0.3,
with occasional excursions to +/-3. Nothing a reader could name predicts it well. The
current token's identity explains only about 1% of its variance, the classes of the
preceding tokens (words, punctuation, code, digits) explain essentially nothing, and
position within a document explains nothing. The one reliable fact is at the start of a
document (and at a row's first token), where the component is exactly silent: its
activation there is about 0.

So the program says: silent (0) at the first token of each document, and otherwise the
component's average value (0.038) everywhere. It captures the mean and the silence at
document starts; it does not capture the token-by-token wobble.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.038
"""The component's average activation over training text, positions after a document's first token."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first_in_document = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if first_in_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 3718 (component p-82af68dd ... down_proj:3718), read as a
word-level rule.

This component is one rank-one piece of layer 15's down projection, and its input
direction is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 3718. Its activation is mostly small and
noisy, and most of its variance is not explained by any simple word-level rule: token
identity and short-window word counts explain well under 1% of it on held-out text.

Its clearest pattern is negative values in clauses about affecting, preventing,
protecting or causing something: on the verb itself ("protect", "prevent", "cause",
"impact", "ensure", "maintain", ...) and on the small function word that opens the
object of such a verb ("to prevent [the] water", "protect [the] devices", "affecting
[the] ..."). Its largest negative values (below -5) are mostly these function words.
Everywhere else the program predicts 0.

Put into the model in place of the component, this rule moves the output very little,
as the component itself does.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Verbs of affecting, preventing, protecting or causing something.
EFFECT_VERBS = frozenset(
    """
    prevent prevents prevented preventing protect protects protected protecting
    cause causes caused causing affect affects affected affecting impact impacts
    impacted impacting interfere interferes interfering ensure ensures ensured
    maintain maintains keep keeps harm harms damage damages ruin ruins block blocks
    hinder hinders disrupt disrupts minimize minimise reduce threaten threatens
    avoid avoids limit limits
    """.split()
)

# Small words that open the object or complement of such a verb.
OBJECT_WORDS = frozenset(
    """
    the a an to of on into over from with in that it your my their its his her our
    """.split()
)

WINDOW = 3  # how many earlier words to look back over, within the same document
ON_EFFECT_VERB = -0.4  # on the effect verb itself
ON_OBJECT_WORD = -0.6  # on an object word just after an effect verb


def _word(text: str) -> str:
    return text.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[t]
    word = _word(prefix.token_strings[t])
    earlier = [
        _word(prefix.token_strings[i])
        for i in range(max(0, t - WINDOW), t)
        if prefix.document_ids[i] == doc
    ]
    if word in EFFECT_VERBS:
        value = ON_EFFECT_VERB
    elif word in OBJECT_WORDS and any(w in EFFECT_VERBS for w in earlier):
        value = ON_OBJECT_WORD
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3719: a weak, diffuse direction in the layer-15 MLP.

What it does: its activation is a fixed weighted sum of the 6144 MLP hidden units of
layer 15. No small set of tokens or word classes predicts it: the best token-identity
table, with about 1000 entries, explains about 1% of its variance out of sample. Its
sign and size depend on context the token alone does not show. Its contribution is
about 0.5% of its MLP's output, and switching it off changes the model's next-token
predictions by almost nothing.

What this program keeps: the one clear regularity we found. Markup and
machine-formatting tokens (tags such as </tool_call>, JSON-style '":', backslash
escapes) are on average pushed negative. Everything else, including the first token
of each document, is predicted as 0. The program explains almost none of the variance
(eval: variance explained 0.00017, r 0.02) and is meant as a readable description,
not a good predictor.
"""

import re

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MARKUP = re.compile(r'[<>]|":|\\')
MARKUP_VALUE = -0.1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    if MARKUP.search(prefix.token_strings[-1]):
        return carry, MARKUP_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 3721: a diffuse, mostly-zero-mean feature.

What it is: this component's input direction is dominated by MLP hidden unit 3721 of
layer 15 (about 44 percent of its input energy sits on that unit), so its activation
tracks that neuron (correlation about 0.6 on sampled tokens). Its activation is signed,
roughly symmetric around 0, and spread over ordinary text and code alike.

What the program does: it predicts the activation's mean, a constant near zero, at every
position. Nothing readable in the tokens predicts it: no token class, no bracket or
identifier context, and no token identity (a per-token lookup table explains only about
2 percent of its variance, and that needs a 20,000-entry table, which is not a concept).

So this program explains almost nothing. It is the honest baseline: the component's
signal is not captured by any short rule we found.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.0123


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 3723 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3723).

Its activation is dominated by MLP hidden unit 3723 of layer 15 (about 60% of its
variance; the rest is spread over many small units). In the text it is most negative
on words about where and how people live: home,
house, live, stay, living, room, bed, camp, prison, apartment, wife, life, alone.
It is mildly positive on words that set up a verb or a hypothetical: modals and
subject pronouns (could, would, had, were, he, they), and words such as being,
born, because. Everything else sits near zero.

The program predicts the activation from the newest word alone, with a fixed value
per word class. It captures only a little of the variance: most of the activation is
context-dependent and not carried by any single word.
"""

READS = ()

# Words about dwelling, living conditions and confinement: the negative side.
HOME_WORDS = frozenset(
    "home house houses live lived lives living stay stayed stays room rooms bed beds "
    "camp prison apartment residents quarters cabin tent shelter wife life alone "
    "comfort comfortable".split()
)

# Modals, auxiliaries and subject pronouns, which a verb tends to follow: the positive side.
VERB_CUE_WORDS = frozenset(
    "could would can had have were was who when because being born person "
    "he she they i you".split()
)

HOME_VALUE = -1.0
VERB_CUE_VALUE = 0.15


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in HOME_WORDS:
        return carry, HOME_VALUE
    if word in VERB_CUE_WORDS:
        return carry, VERB_CUE_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3724 (layer 15 MLP down_proj).

What it does: a near-silent direction in the MLP's hidden space. Its activation is
(hidden . V_c) * |U_c|, and across the training corpus it is diffuse: it has no token
concept (the best token-identity table explains about 3% of its variance, and simple
token classes such as punctuation, capitals, leading spaces or CJK explain under 0.2%).
It is also almost never important (CI ~ 4e-7), so switching it off barely changes the output.

What this program predicts: the only regularity that is consistent across documents is
at the start of a document. The first token reads about 0, the second and third tokens
read slightly positive, and everything later sits at the corpus mean of about -0.005.
Positions count from each document's first token; a row packs several documents, and
the count restarts where the document label changes.
"""

READS = ()

# activation by position within the document; anything not listed is the corpus mean
EARLY_POSITION = {0: 0.0, 1: 0.09, 2: 0.07, 3: 0.03, 4: 0.025}
CORPUS_MEAN = -0.005


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        n = 0
    else:
        n = carry[1] + 1
    return (doc, n), EARLY_POSITION.get(n, CORPUS_MEAN)

"""Predicts a constant: the component's average activation, about 0.02, at every position.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:3725 is one rank-one piece of layer 15's
MLP down-projection. Its input direction is spread over many hidden units (hidden unit 3725
carries the largest share), and its output is small: it never passes the harvest's
causal-importance threshold, and switching it off barely changes the model's predictions.

What the activation does look like, measured on 16k training rows:
- It is roughly symmetric around 0 (std 0.32, mean 0.02), with a little positive lean in the
  first few tokens of a document and about 0 on the first token itself.
- No readable token property explains it. The current token's identity explains about 1-2% of
  its variance on held-out rows (and that needs a 150k-entry table); the previous token, the
  bigram, the token's character class (word, digits, punctuation, non-ASCII) and the position
  each explain under 0.1%.
- It varies slowly within a document (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.36), but a running average of
  token-level features does not track it either.

So the program predicts the typical value. It is the simplest honest answer: it does not
claim a trigger the component does not have.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0216


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Time-span / duration neuron (v5).

Layer 15, MLP unit 3726 (the component reads almost only that unit) is high on words that name
or extend a span of time, in many languages: 'years', 'weeks', 'season', 'period', 'long',
'stayed', 'remained', 'long-term', 'temporary', 'anos', 'années', '期間', '长期', '一直'.
It is also high on the small words that continue such a phrase: the preposition right after a
span word ('weeks of', 'years in', 'days at') and the article after a span-introducing word
('during the', 'throughout the'). It is negative on words of sequence and speed ('already',
'before', 'subsequently', 'eventually', '已经', '慢慢', '未来'). Most of its variance is in contexts
no word list reaches, so this predicts only what a word list and these two rules can see.
"""
READS = ()

SPAN_NOUNS = set("""year years month months week weeks day days hour hours season seasons period periods
decade decades century centuries lifetime duration term night nights -year -years -term -day -days
-week -weeks -month -months -decade anos año años meses mes semanas semana dias días tempo tiempo
année années mois jours semaine durée jahre jahren monate tage woche wochen zeit anni giorni
czas лет года дней время""".split())
SPAN_CJK = ("期間", "期间", "長期", "长期", "一直", "多年", "持久", "永久", "時間")
DURATION_WORDS = set("""long longer stay stays stayed remain remains remained temporary temporarily
persistent permanent permanently lasting prolonged sustained continue continued continues while
overnight brief briefly forever indefinitely lifelong chronic durante lange durée долго""".split())
WEAK_TIME = set("""time been minutes always spent kept keep maintain temps""".split())
SEQUENCE = set("""already before subsequently subsequent eventually gradually rapidly rapid prevent
preventing later spontaneous soon afterwards afterward slowly quickly further""".split())
SEQUENCE_CJK = ("已经", "已", "慢慢", "快速", "之前", "进一步", "不断", "及时", "未来")
PREP_AFTER_SPAN = set("of in at on with after as".split())
INTRO_SPAN = set("during throughout while within leaving maintaining keep keeping leave hold maintain joined left".split())
ARTICLE = set("the this its our their his her a".split())


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (span context from earlier tokens, whether the previous token was a span word)
    ctx, prev_span, prev_intro = (0.0, False, False) if carry is None else carry
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        ctx, prev_span, prev_intro = 0.0, False, False
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    is_span = word in SPAN_NOUNS or word in SPAN_CJK
    is_dur = word in DURATION_WORDS
    if is_span:
        own, hit = 3.0, 1.0
    elif is_dur:
        own, hit = 2.5, 1.0
    elif word in WEAK_TIME:
        own, hit = 1.5, 0.5
    elif word in SEQUENCE or word in SEQUENCE_CJK:
        own, hit = -1.5, 0.0
    else:
        own, hit = 0.0, 0.0
    if prev_span and word in PREP_AFTER_SPAN:
        own = max(own, 4.0)
    if prev_intro and word in ARTICLE:
        own = max(own, 2.0)
    value = 0.7 * (own + ctx)
    return (0.5 * ctx + hit, is_span or is_dur, word in INTRO_SPAN), value

"""Predicts layer 15 MLP unit 3727 (down_proj component) of Qwen3-1.7B.

The unit is a "be-verb" detector. It is strongly active on forms of the English verb
"to be" that sit between a subject and its predicate or passive participle: was, were,
been, be, being, are, is, am, 're, 'm. Their foreign equivalents (été, être, est, ist,
sono, был, sont) give a smaller response. It is weaker when the subject is an
expletive ("there is", "it was", "this is"). It is weakly positive on frequency and
manner adverbs that come between a subject and its verb (often, usually, typically,
originally) and on "not". Everywhere else it sits near zero.

Its output direction weakly favours predicate words after a "be" verb (able, active,
achievable), so it marks the slot where a predicate or passive participle comes next.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

ENGLISH_BE = {
    " be", " been", " being", " is", " was", " were", " are", " am",
    " BE", " IS", " Is", " Are", " Was", "was", "Are", "’re", "'re", "’m", "'m",
}  # fmt: skip
OTHER_BE = {
    " être", " été", " était", " est", " é", " sont", " ist", " sind", " ser",
    " sono", " era", " був", " был", " была", " быть", " zijn", " são", " waren",
    " wurde", " worden", " foi", " fut", " jest",
}  # fmt: skip
ADVERBS = {
    " often", " typically", " usually", " originally", " initially", " widely",
    " commonly", " previously", " primarily", " currently", " frequently",
    " sometimes", " always", " specifically", " officially", " briefly",
    " actually", " significantly", " mostly", " subsequently", " generally",
    " normally", " traditionally",
}  # fmt: skip
EXPLETIVES = {" there", " There", " it", " It", " this", " This"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The unit's activation at the newest token of the prefix."""
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if token in ENGLISH_BE:
        return carry, 2.6 if before in EXPLETIVES else 5.0
    if token in OTHER_BE:
        return carry, 2.0
    if token in ADVERBS:
        return carry, 1.3
    if token == " not":
        return carry, 1.1
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 3728 (down_proj component 3728 reads almost only that unit):
a "part-of / partitive" detector.

It fires on the function word that opens a partitive or part-whole phrase. Mostly "of"
("the bottom of", "84 percent of", "the characteristics of"), then "in", "on", "into",
"within" and "per", and the quantifiers and possessives "all", "each", "every", "most",
"both", "your", "our" ("all of", "each of", "your ..."). It fires about twice as hard when
a part, aspect or quantity noun (side, edge, percent, portion, feature, ...) sits within
the three words before it. After a capitalised word ("City of", "University of") "of"
drops to its resting value. Everywhere else it sits at the component's mean, -0.06.
Measured on eval: variance explained about 0.05, correlation 0.22; zeroing it moves the
model about as much as this program does.
"""

READS = ()

# Part, aspect and quantity nouns: what an "of" or "in" usually follows.
PART = {"percent", "portion", "part", "side", "edge", "surface", "bottom", "top", "back", "section",
        "majority", "half", "structure", "feature", "characteristic", "aspect", "component", "content",
        "nature", "description", "center", "boundary", "core", "base", "parameter", "property", "element",
        "percentage", "fraction", "number", "amount", "type", "kind", "level", "layer"}

# Typical activation of each function word, in the component's units.
PREP = {"of": 1.2, "in": 0.5, "on": 0.6, "into": 0.6, "within": 1.0, "between": 0.5, "for": 0.2, "per": 0.9}
DET = {"all": 1.2, "each": 1.1, "every": 1.0, "most": 1.1, "both": 0.5, "many": 0.5,
       "your": 0.8, "our": 0.7, "their": 0.5, "my": 0.5}

REST = -0.06  # the component's mean activation everywhere else


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    words = [s.strip().lower() for s in prefix.token_strings[-4:]]
    w = words[-1]
    base = PREP.get(w, DET.get(w, REST))
    if w == "the":
        base = 0.1
    if base <= 0:
        return carry, REST
    if any(x in PART for x in words[:-1]):
        base *= 2.0
    if w == "of" and len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2].strip()[:1].isupper():
        base = REST
    return carry, base

"""Component layer 15 MLP down_proj:3730 — a weak, diffuse, mostly context-driven signal.

The component reads MLP hidden unit 3730 of layer 15, and that unit alone accounts for
about 40% of its variance; the rest is spread over thousands of small terms.

What the program does: the activation is on average highest on comparison operators
(>=, <=, >, <, ≥, ≤, ==, !=; mean about +0.4) and on limit / threshold / time words
(exceed, limit, threshold, timeout, less, than, least, sleep, interval; mean about +0.27),
moderately positive on arithmetic operators (mean about +0.1), slightly negative on digits
(mean about -0.04), and close to its overall mean (about +0.02) elsewhere. The program
predicts the mean activation of the current token's group, read from that token's text.

Why this is all it does: no token-level description captures much of the variance. Group
means explain under 1% of it on training text; a per-token lookup table reaches only a
few percent, and the best context-window models I fit reach about 4%. Individual top
activations are diverse (keyword-argument names before '=', arithmetic in time
expressions such as 1000 * 60 *, comparisons, timeouts), but none of these concepts
accounts for much of the total.
"""

READS = ()

COMPARISON = {"<", ">", "<=", ">=", "≤", "≥", "==", "!="}
LIMIT_TIME = {
    "exceed", "exceeds", "exceeding", "limit", "limits", "threshold", "timeout",
    "below", "least", "less", "greater", "than", "sleep", "interval", "delay",
    "max", "maximum",
}

# Mean activation per token group, measured on training text.
MEAN = {
    "comparison": 0.39,
    "limit_time": 0.27,
    "arith": 0.10,
    "dot_method": 0.05,
    "bracket": 0.05,
    "newline": 0.07,
    "space": 0.04,
    "digit": -0.04,
    "word": 0.02,
    "other": 0.03,
}


def group(token):
    """The group of a token, from its text alone."""
    w = token.strip().lower()
    if w in COMPARISON:
        return "comparison"
    if w in LIMIT_TIME:
        return "limit_time"
    if w.startswith(".") and len(w) > 1:
        return "dot_method"

"""Layout detector for source code: negative at the blank lines and indentation that open blocks.

On ordinary words, digits and single spaces the component is near zero. It goes negative on the
layout of code:
  - the first indentation after a blank line, which opens a new block (strongest), and a
    declaration keyword (`import`, `def`, `public`, `#`, `//`) starting a line after a blank line;
  - a blank line itself, most of all one that ends a statement (`;`, `)`, `}`) in code, and a
    tab-indented blank line;
  - a declaration keyword at the start of an ordinary line in code;
  - indentation at the start of a line, more for tabs than for spaces;
  - comment markers (`*`, `//`) starting a line.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Declaration keywords and comment openers.
OPENERS = {"import", "def", "class", "public", "private", "void", "int", "func", "fn", "#", "//"}

# Comment markers that start a line.
MARKERS = {"*", "//", "///", "#", "-", ">"}

# Characters that end a statement or block in code.
CODE_END = set(";{})]")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if prefix.position > 0 else ""
    newlines = tok.count("\n")  # line breaks in this token
    after_blank = prev.count("\n") >= 2  # the previous token ended a blank line
    after_break = prev.count("\n") == 1  # the previous token ended a line
    line_start = after_break or (prev != "" and prev.strip(" \t") == "")  # after a break or indent
    indent = newlines == 0 and len(tok) >= 2 and tok.strip(" \t") == ""  # a run of indentation
    tab = "\t" in tok
    word = tok.strip()

    if newlines >= 2:  # a blank line
        return carry, (-9.0 if tok.rstrip("\n \t")[-1:] in CODE_END else -4.0)
    if after_blank:  # the first token of a line after a blank line
        if indent:
            return carry, -20.0
        if word in OPENERS:
            return carry, -11.0
        return carry, -1.7
    if newlines == 1 and tab:  # a tab-indented blank line
        return carry, -16.0
    if line_start and word in OPENERS:  # a declaration keyword starting a line
        return carry, -5.0
    if indent:  # indentation at the start of a line, or mid-line
        return carry, (-5.0 if tab else -2.0)
    if after_break and word in MARKERS:  # a comment marker starting a line
        return carry, -3.0
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 3738.

What it does, in plain terms: this component goes strongly negative when the text is in
type-signature territory: code or formal maths where the next word is likely a type or
type-level construct (`typedef`, `<T>`, `Type u`, `typeof`, `Generic`, `interface`, Lean
goal states with `⊢` and `inst✝`, Haskell `Vector v a =>`). Its negative sign pushes the
residual toward type words (`type`, `types`, `typedef`, `类型`). It stays near zero in
everyday prose and arithmetic, and is mildly positive there.

The program predicts it from two signals that it reads from the text so far:
  * the current token is a type word (large negative), and
  * how much type vocabulary the recent text has had (an exponentially decaying average
    over the document, so it fades over roughly ten tokens),
plus a weaker pair of the same two signals for formal-maths markers.
Document boundaries reset the memory, as the model's attention does.

Fit by least squares on 16k training rows; the coefficients are rounded.
"""

import re

READS = ()

TYPE_WORD = re.compile(
    r"type|Type|TYPE|typ|Generic|generic|Interface|interface|Struct|struct|Enum|enum|Class|class"
)
FORMAL_MARK = re.compile(r"⊢|✝|∀|∃|ℕ|ℝ|ℤ|ℚ|ℂ|∈|⊆|→|::|=>|:=|\\|\$|theorem|lemma|Prop|Set|Module|instance|where")
DECAY = 0.9  # per-token memory of the recent text


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        type_mem, formal_mem = 0.0, 0.0  # a new document starts with no memory
    else:
        _, type_mem, formal_mem = carry
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    is_type = 1.0 if TYPE_WORD.search(token) else 0.0
    is_formal = 1.0 if FORMAL_MARK.search(token) else 0.0
    value = (
        -1.1 * is_type
        - 5.0 * type_mem
        - 0.1 * is_formal
        - 0.8 * formal_mem
    )
    type_mem = DECAY * type_mem + (1 - DECAY) * is_type
    formal_mem = DECAY * formal_mem + (1 - DECAY) * is_formal
    return (doc, type_mem, formal_mem), value

The component's activation is diffuse and context-dependent. The only token-level
signal I found is weak: the average value differs a little between kinds of
token. Punctuation that follows a space, and digits, sit slightly above average.
Plain lowercase words sit slightly below. Position 0 of a row is always about 0.
Explaining the variance here needs far more than token kind, so this program
predicts small per-kind offsets and is only a little better than a constant.

READS = ()

OTHER = 0.019
PUNCT_AFTER_SPACE = 0.06
DIGIT = 0.035
WORD = -0.005
WORD_AFTER_SPACE = 0.019

    if prefix.position == 0:

    if regex.fullmatch(r"\s*\p{Nd}+", s):

words ("enough", "nonetheless") when it is negative and diminishing words

higher in software-flavoured text: code identifiers and file paths (snake_case, CamelCase,

  - a running "technical register": how much of the recent text (decaying over about 10
    tokens, reset at each new document) was identifiers or software words;
  - whether the current token is an identifier, and whether it is a software word;
  - whether it is code punctuation, and whether it is a line break.

current token reaches only about 6%, so most of this component is not captured by a readable
rule.

SOFTWARE_WORDS = {
    "test", "tests", "testing", "spec", "should", "error", "errors", "warning",
    "warn", "exception", "fail", "failed", "failure", "config", "configuration",
    "parse", "parser", "parsing", "serialize", "schema", "validate", "validation",
    "invalid", "request", "response", "handler", "middleware", "module", "import",
    "function", "default", "init", "initialize", "build", "compile", "runtime",
    "cache", "server", "client", "api", "route", "json", "yaml", "template",
    "resource", "resources", "deprecated", "undefined", "null", "callback",
    "async", "await", "lint", "loader", "render", "context", "options", "instance",
}

    """A code-style name: has a letter and '_', '::', '/', a dot before a letter, or camelCase."""
    t = text.strip()
    return bool(re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", t)) and bool(
        re.search(r"_|::|/|\.[A-Za-z_]|[a-z][A-Z]|->", t))


def is_software_word(text):
    t = text.strip().lower().strip("_./:")
    return t in SOFTWARE_WORDS or (len(t) > 2 and t.startswith(SOFTWARE_STEMS))

    t = text.strip()

             - 0.115 * is_code_punct(text)
             - 0.171 * ("\n" in text))
    return level * DECAY + techy * (1 - DECAY), float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection component 3765: a "line break or closing bracket" feature.

The component's activation is a token-level signal. It is large and positive on
  - line breaks: whitespace tokens that contain a newline (strongest),
  - closing delimiters: ")", "]", "}", a closing quote (" ” '), backtick, "$", ">" (and "$$", "」"),
  - backslashes, as in code or in the written escape "\\n",
and moderately positive on plain spaces and indents. It is near zero on words and
digits, and about zero on most other punctuation.

This program reads only the newest token and returns one value per token from these
classes. Tokens that open something (' "', '("', '{"') are not closers. Line breaks
that follow a sentence or code punctuation mark (".\\n", ";\\n", ":\\n") are merged
into one token by the tokenizer and read as punctuation, so they stay near zero.
What it leaves out: the size of a line break varies with its context (larger in
running prose, smaller in code), and each token has its own typical size, which a
per-token table would capture.
"""

READS = ()

CLOSERS = set(')]}"”`$」）】》>')
BACKSLASHES = ("\\", " \\", "\\n", "\\\\")

NEWLINE_VALUE = 8.5  # whitespace-only token containing a newline
SPACE_VALUE = 2.7  # other whitespace-only token (space, indent)
CLOSER_VALUE = 4.9  # token made only of closing delimiters, optionally a newline
BACKSLASH_VALUE = 4.3  # backslash tokens
DIGIT_VALUE = -0.3  # digit tokens
WORD_VALUE = -0.1  # tokens containing letters
OTHER_VALUE = 0.1  # the rest of the punctuation


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if tok.strip() == "":
        return carry, (NEWLINE_VALUE if "\n" in tok else SPACE_VALUE)
    if tok.strip() in BACKSLASHES:
        return carry, BACKSLASH_VALUE
    body = tok[:-1] if tok.endswith("\n") else tok
    if body and not body[0].isspace() and all(c in CLOSERS for c in body):
        return carry, CLOSER_VALUE
    if body.isdigit():
        return carry, DIGIT_VALUE
    if any(c.isalpha() for c in body):
        return carry, WORD_VALUE
    return carry, OTHER_VALUE

"""Rare, unfamiliar capitalised words: names and terms the model has not seen often.

The component is a hidden unit of layer 15's MLP, read out through one output direction.
Its value is usually near zero (median 0.14) and has a heavy upper tail. The tail is mostly
the first token of a capitalised name or technical term in running English text, where the
next token continues the name ("... the Wall" + " Street", "... at Harvey"); it is largest
after a preposition or article and for rare words, and smaller for later words of a name.
Common words (the, water, of, a sentence-initial The) predict about 0. Rare lowercase word
starts give a small value.

What this leaves out: the many ordinary tokens where the unit dips below zero, and the
word-internal fragments of split words, which need the next token. It explains about 4-5%
of the variance.

Rarity is 1 for a word that wordfreq rates rare in English (Zipf below about 5) and 0 for a
common one, so the value depends on how familiar the word is, not on its exact spelling.
"""
import math
import re

import wordfreq

READS = ()

BASELINE = 0.1  # typical value for punctuation, digits and other non-word tokens
CJK_VALUE = 0.4  # Han characters, which often start a multi-character word


def rarity(word):
    """1 for a rare word, 0 for a very common one (a smooth step at Zipf frequency 5)."""
    zipf = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word.lower(), "en")
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(zipf - 5))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = token.strip()
    if re.search(r"[一-鿿]", token):
        return carry, CJK_VALUE
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[^\W\d_]+", word):
        return carry, BASELINE
    leads = token.startswith(" ")
    capital = word[0].isupper()
    # Capitalised words after a space open names and titles most strongly.
    shape = 0.3 + (1.2 if capital and leads else 0.0) + (0.4 if leads else 0.0) + (0.8 if capital and not leads else 0.0)
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if prev[:1].isupper():
        shape *= 0.5  # later words of a name are weaker than the first
    return carry, shape * rarity(word) + 0.09

"""Colon detector: a component of layers.15.mlp.down_proj that fires on the colon
that introduces a label, value or explanation ("Joined:", "Example:", "Error:",
"note:", "file:"), and is nearly silent on ordinary text.

What it does, in plain terms:
- On a colon ":" (or the full-width "："), it predicts a large activation. The
  first colon in a document is strongest (about 4.4); each earlier colon in the
  same document lowers it, settling near 2 after many, so repeated "Label:"
  lines and "case 1:" lists are weaker than a new label.
- A colon right after a digit ("12:30", "1:") is weaker: half that.
- Colon-ending tokens such as ":\\n", ":\\n\\n", "):" and '":' are smaller.
- The space that follows a label colon ("Posts: 56") is slightly active.
- Every other token predicts 0. Ordinary words and punctuation carry small,
  unpredictable activations that this program does not model.

Attention resets at document boundaries, so the program counts colons from the
start of each document only.
"""
import math
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Typical activation of colon-ending tokens other than a plain colon.
OTHER_COLON_LEVEL = {":\n": 1.5, ":\n\n": 1.9, "):": 2.2, '":': 1.1, " :": 0.9}
FULLWIDTH_COLON = "："


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = len(prefix.token_ids) - 1
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, t, 0)  # a new document starts here, with no colons yet
    _, start, earlier = carry
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if t > start else ""

    if tok in (":", FULLWIDTH_COLON):
        # Drops with each earlier colon in the document: 4.4, then toward 1.8.
        value = 1.8 + 2.6 * 0.7**earlier
        if prev[-1:].isdigit():
            value *= 0.5  # "12:30", "case 1:"
        if tok == FULLWIDTH_COLON:
            value *= 1.2
        earlier += 1
    elif tok in OTHER_COLON_LEVEL:
        value = OTHER_COLON_LEVEL[tok]
    elif tok == " " and prev in (":", FULLWIDTH_COLON):
        value = 0.9  # the space after a label colon
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (doc, start, earlier), float(value)

This component reads hidden unit 3769 of layer 15's MLP (about 70% of its input weight is
on that one unit). Its activation is usually near zero with random sign, spread over code
and prose; no token, pair of tokens, bracket depth or repetition predicts its sign. The one

"""Typical activation at such an "=" (median about -11, mean about -14)."""

"""Mild typical activation elsewhere in a document after its first definition."""

This component reads mainly MLP hidden unit 3770 of layer 15 (about 70% of its squared
input norm), so its activation is roughly that unit's value. The unit goes negative in
algebra and arithmetic text:
- on a comma, space or "and" that follows a number, much more so inside brackets, as in
  "(0,0)" or "{1,1}";
- on single-letter variables and operators inside brackets;
- and mildly, wherever the last 8 tokens are dense with maths tokens.
Elsewhere it sits near zero. Its large spikes (down to about -28, often on algebra
pairs) depend on context that these token rules do not capture, so the program explains
only about 1.5% of the variance; it gets the sign and the broad trend right.
"""

MATH_CHARS = set("+-*/=^<>")


def _kind(s):
    t = s.strip()
    if t.isdigit():
        return "num"
    if len(t) == 1 and t.isascii() and t.isalpha():
        return "var"
    if t and set(t) <= MATH_CHARS:
        return "op"
    if t in (",", "and") or (t == "" and "\n" not in s):
        return "sep"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    depth, prev_kind, recent = (0, "", ()) if carry is None or new_doc else carry
    kind = _kind(s)
    # bracket depth before this token; the bracket characters update it afterwards
    inside = depth > 0
    is_math = kind in ("num", "var", "op") or any(c in s for c in "()[]{},")
    recent = (recent + (is_math,))[-8:]
    density = sum(recent) / 8
    value = 0.03
    if kind == "sep" and prev_kind == "num":

    if inside and kind in ("var", "op"):

    value -= 0.25 * density
    depth = max(0, depth + sum(c in "([{" for c in s) - sum(c in ")]}" for c in s))
    return (depth, kind, recent), value

What it does: the component's activation is (hidden unit 3772 of layer 15's MLP) times a
unit-norm output direction, so it is a gated neuron: its gate opens on text where a term is
being spelled out (inside acronyms, names and technical labels), and its sign depends on the
kind of text. Measured on training text, its activation is positive on acronyms (ABC, ZANU-PF),
numbers and symbols, and mildly negative on ordinary lowercase words and on the pieces of a
capitalised name that continue a word.

(an acronym), capitalised, lowercase, a number, punctuation or whitespace, and does it attach
to the previous token (no leading space, so it continues a word). Each (shape, attached) cell
predicts the mean activation measured for it. It explains only about 0.5% of the variance: the
activation is mostly set by context that a token's shape does not show.

from collections.abc import Mapping

MEAN = {
    ("caps", True): 0.34,  # acronym continuing a word, e.g. the "BA" of "EC" + "BA"
    ("caps", False): 0.04,
    ("digit", True): 0.12,  # digits inside a label, e.g. "Level [1]", "Type II"
    ("punct", True): 0.08,
    ("punct", False): 0.14,  # symbols after a space, e.g. " (" or " ="
    ("space", True): 0.01,
    ("space", False): 0.11,
    ("Cap", True): -0.01,  # capitalised name piece glued to a word
    ("Cap", False): 0.03,  # capitalised word starting a new word
    ("lower", True): -0.04,  # ordinary word piece
    ("lower", False): -0.01,
}

SHAPES = (
    (re.compile(r"[A-Z]{2,}[0-9]*"), "caps"),
    (re.compile(r"[A-Z][a-z]*"), "Cap"),
    (re.compile(r"[a-z]+"), "lower"),
    (re.compile(r"[0-9]+"), "digit"),
    (re.compile(r"[^\w\s]+"), "punct"),
)


def shape(text: str) -> str:
    """The character shape of a token's text, ignoring its leading space."""
    body = text.strip()
    if not body:
        return "space"
    for pattern, name in SHAPES:

    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]

Layer 15's MLP hidden unit 3774 (this component's main input) has no simple
token-level driver: token identity, token frequency, position, repetition and
bag-of-recent-words explain well under 1% of its variance. The only consistent
pattern is small: words that begin with a space run slightly higher than
bare words, digits and punctuation. So the program predicts a per-class mean
(all near -0.04), and 0 at the first token of a document.

READS = ()

SPACED_WORD = -0.034  # " word": the most common kind of token
BARE_WORD = -0.062  # "word" with no leading space, e.g. inside a compound
OTHER = -0.04  # digits, punctuation, newlines, CJK and the rest

    doc = prefix.document_ids
    if len(doc) == 1 or doc[-1] != doc[-2]:

    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 3775, as component 3775 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj.

What the component is: its activation is mostly the MLP hidden unit 3775 of layer 15
(its weight on that unit is 0.88, and that unit alone carries about half the variance).
Its large positive values come mostly at a comma or "and"/"or" that continues a list of
descriptive words, as in "tough, tender, [funny]", "sparkly, edgy, [preppy]" or
"intimate, spirited [and] honest".

What this program does: at each position it predicts a small positive value when the
current token is a comma, "and" or "or", larger when an adjective appears in the few
words just before it (WordNet tags the words), and 0 at every other token. It only
looks back within the same document.

Honest limit: the bulk of the activation (sd about 0.47 at ordinary tokens, both signs)
is not explained by surface features. Token identity, neighbouring words, position,
code-ness and repetition each explain about 0.1% of the variance or less. On the eval
rows this program explains about 0.1% of the variance (Pearson r about 0.04).
"""

from wordnet import parts_of_speech

READS = ()

SEPARATORS = {",", "and", "or"}
LOOKBACK = 3  # words before a separator searched for an adjective


def _word(token):
    return token.strip().lower()


def _is_adjective(token):
    word = _word(token)
    return word.isalpha() and "adjective" in parts_of_speech(word)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    i = len(prefix.token_ids) - 1
    if _word(prefix.token_strings[i]) not in SEPARATORS:
        return carry, 0.0
    # only look back within the same document
    start = max(0, i - LOOKBACK)
    before = [
        j
        for j in range(start, i)
        if prefix.document_ids[j] == prefix.document_ids[i]
    ]
    if before and _is_adjective(prefix.token_strings[before[-1]]):
        value = 0.27  # directly after an adjective: "tough, tender, [funny]"
    elif any(_is_adjective(prefix.token_strings[j]) for j in before):
        value = 0.17  # an adjective a word or two back
    else:
        value = 0.09  # any other comma, "and" or "or"
    return carry, value
